### p6
*2026-08-25 12:20*

> question: can I install the same pwa twice on my phone, and have each one log in as a different user? similar question: multiple users in different browser tabs on the mac?

Short answer: yes to both, with caveats. Let me check one detail — how the app decides whether to show install instructions vs. the real app — so I'm precise about the Mac case.

**On the phone: yes.** iOS gives every home-screen web app its own storage container — cookies, localStorage, caches, service worker — separate from Safari and from every other icon, even when they point at the same URL. So "Add to Home Screen" twice gives you two icons, each starting logged out, and each can hold a different `miso_auth` cookie. Nothing in miso ties identity to the device: the session is a cookie, the per-user world is keyed server-side by the logged-in user, and passkeys are per-account so each instance can enrol its own Face ID. Two caveats:

- The two icons look identical. You'd want a distinguishing name — that's a display-name / profile thing, and today's work could easily make the installed app's badge or profile say who it is.
- **The login code goes to the account's phone number**, so on your phone you can only be a second person whose SMS you receive. For a demo that's the `_`-prefixed test users (PIN to the server log, no SMS) — e.g. a `_tara` entry you log in as from the second icon. Real Tara logs in on real Tara's phone.

**On the Mac: yes, but not per tab.** Cookies belong to the browser profile, not the tab — two tabs in the same Safari share one `miso_auth`, so logging in on one logs both in. Separate users need separate cookie jars: different browsers (Safari + Chrome + Firefox = three users), Chrome profiles, or a private window (its own jar until closed). Desktop browsers skip the install wall and get the real app, so this works today with no changes.

One thing this surfaces for the accounts work: the rig-proven way to test multi-user flows on one machine is exactly this (a fresh browser profile per user), which is how the contexts ladder was tested. I'd use it for the invite → directory proof today.

### p8
*2026-08-25 12:29*

> OK, so I quite like the idea that users own their data, and exchange it back and forth

That changes the shape, and I think for the better. Let me say back what I think you mean and what it does to the plan.

**The idea:** your profile — name, picture, mission — is *yours*: it lives in your own world, the same per-user world your ticks and tunables live in. Nobody reads it there. Other people see it because you **send them a copy**, and you see theirs because they sent you one. A "directory" isn't a list on the server; it's the cards people have handed you. A link is the two of you having exchanged cards. Same for projects and roles: "Ash is lead developer for app" is a card in my world; the project's page shows it because I sent it to the project.

**Why I like it:**

- It's the machinery we already have. Per-user worlds exist, the op log exists, `/messaging` already relays to a world's owner, the chooser already "sends a feature" by flipping a switch. What's missing is one primitive: *copy this var from my world into yours, with consent* — and that's exactly the `share` rung's mechanism, arriving early. No new public store.
- It's the campaign's privacy story for free. Political data is special-category; "every user holds their own data, others hold only what they were given, delete your world and you're gone" is a defensible sentence in front of the party. Rings become "who I've sent this to."
- It's consensual by construction. Nobody appears in your directory without handing you a card, so unwanted contact is structurally impossible — the constraint notes.md wanted at birth.

**Two honest caveats:**

- *Owning* doesn't mean the server has no copy — the mini holds every world. Ownership here means: only you write it, others hold copies only by your act, and you can withdraw it (your world is yours to delete). Worth saying plainly to Tara rather than implying the server is blind.
- A **project** needs to be somebody's. Simplest: the creator's world holds it, and the project's members are the accept-set of people who exchanged cards with it. "A group is the set of people who accepted" — the ruling already in notes.md.
- Queries ("who has role R in X?") run over what *you* hold. That's the feature, but it means a campaign lead sees the whole team only because the whole team sent them cards. For a campaign that's fine and probably right.

**Reframed step 1:** the 👤 page, editable — name, picture (downscaled on-device, stored as a var), mission — living in your world. Plus a **"send my card"** action and a **"people"** list of cards you've received. Exchange first, directory falls out of it. Then step 2, projects, is a card-with-roles you send to a project.

Want me to build it this way? One question in your language: when Tara sends you her card, is that it (she appears in your people list), or do you get an "accept" tap first?

### p9
*2026-08-25 12:31*

> OK, so there's a basic object here which is a "card", right? It's the same for a post, for a profile, for a group, etc. We have a bunch of cards, and links between them; and cards are 1-5 phone screens long.

Yes — that's the substrate, and it's the same conclusion notes.md reached from the other direction ("everyone gets a page, and a page is a post"). One object, many kinds. Let me pin it down so we're building the same thing:

**A card** is:
- **owned** — it lives in one person's world; copies travel by exchange
- **a kind** — profile, post, project, … a label, not a schema
- **a body of blocks**, in order — title, picture, paragraph, later location/audio/video. The 1–5 screens rule says a card is a *page*, not a row: you open it and scroll, and blocks are the unit of editing
- **linked** — links are typed and go card → card: "role *lead developer* in", "member of", "reply to", "about". "Ash is lead developer for app" is a link from my profile card to the app's project card, carrying the role as its label. The interrogable database is just cards + links
- **time-stamped, id'd**, so a copy can be recognised as the same card and a newer copy replaces an older one

Then everything you listed is a kind: a **profile** is your card about you; a **project** is a card about a thing to get done, whose members are the profile cards linked to it; a **post** is a card with a location and a ring; a **group** is a project without the "get done" flavour. The 👤 page is "my profile card, editable". A directory is "profile cards I hold". A project page is "the project card plus every card linked to it that I hold."

**What that does to today:** step 1 is really three nodes, and the first one is the foundation:

1. **`card`** — the object and its store in your world, render a card as a scrolling page of blocks, edit a block in place. Kind-agnostic.
2. **`profile`** — your own card: kind `profile`, blocks name / picture / mission, opened by 👤, editable because it's yours.
3. **`exchange`** — send a card to a person; cards you've received appear in a **people** list. (Accept-or-not is the question I asked; I'll default to no accept step — a received card just arrives, since only guest-list members can send.)

Projects and links come next — the same `card` node plus a `link` node, no new substrate.

Placement: `miso` is at six children and cards are a root-level thing (data, not shell, not loop), so I'll regroup `comms` and `diag` under an `ops` grouping node and add `cards` as a root child — provenance-neutral, `--chains` diff to prove it. That's a code-level call, so it's mine; I'm telling you so it isn't a surprise.

### p11
*2026-08-25 12:33*

> also, what's interesting is: our dictaphone tool draws a grid of thumbnails for recordings (audio + transcript) - I'd argue that those recordings are cards, in prototype.

Yes — and that's a useful test of the object. A recording is a card of type `recording`: blocks are an audio clip and its transcript, owned by whoever recorded it, in their world, mirrored to the server. Two things the dictaphone already shows that the `cards` node should take as requirements rather than invent:

- **A card has two renderings**: the *thumbnail* (what sits in a grid or a list — the `.crow` row, the tile) and the *page* (the 1–5 screens you open into). The dictaphone grid is a card list; tapping a tile should open the card. Profiles in the people list, projects in a projects list, recordings in the dictaphone — all the same grid of the same thumbnails, filtered by type.
- **Blocks can be blobs.** The audio lives in IndexedDB on the device and travels via `/mirror`; a profile picture is the same problem at smaller size. So a block is either inline text or a reference to a blob stored beside the card, and the mirror path is the exchange path in prototype.

And the migration is the absorption-ladder move we've done before: `dictate` keeps working as is, the `cards` store arrives beside it, recordings get mirrored into it as cards, and only then does the dictaphone grid become "cards of type recording" and the old store retires. Nothing breaks on the way.

So the `cards` node's spec now says: card = `{id, owner, type, created, edited, blocks[], links[]}`, block = text or blob ref, two renderers (tile, page), in-place edit for the owner, the store in your world. Profile, project, recording are values of `type`; the dictaphone is the standing precedent for the tile grid and the blob path.

Say go and I'll start; or keep going if there's more shape to find.

### p19
*2026-08-25 13:20*

> I'd like to look at the user card edit workflow next

Let me read the page half as shipped, so I can describe the edit workflow accurately and say where it's weak.

Here's how it works right now, in plain terms, and where I think it's weak.

**As shipped (build 268)**

1. Tap 👤 → your card appears: name at the top, a picture box, a paragraph box. Empty ones show a grey hint ("your name", "say what you are here to do").
2. Tap the name or the paragraph → it becomes editable in place, border goes dusty blue, keyboard comes up. Type.
3. Tap anywhere else → focus leaves the block, and *that* is the save: the text is sent as a `CardEdit` event and lands in your world. No button, no "saved" message.
4. Tap the picture box → the phone's photo chooser opens; the picture is shrunk to 256px on the phone and stored. If it can't be shrunk under the cap you get a short note ("that picture is too big to keep").

**Where it's weak**

- **A repaint can eat your draft.** Every loop event redraws the whole screen (`$('app').innerHTML = …`). If anything fires while you're mid-sentence — an op arriving from another device, the join, a toolbar tap — the block you're typing in is replaced and the unsaved text is gone, silently: a removed element doesn't reliably fire the "focus left" save. On one device, alone, you'll rarely hit it; with two devices or a busy world you will.
- **Saving is invisible.** "Tap away to keep" is a good rule but nobody's told it; there's no moment where the app says "kept". Silence is our default, but silence about *whether your words are safe* is the wrong silence.
- **Small phone things**: Enter in the name field inserts a line break (a title shouldn't wrap on purpose); there's no way to cancel an edit; and the picture is only replaceable, never removable.

**What I'd change** (small, all inside `cards`): save as you type — send the edit a moment after you stop typing, not only on tap-away — so a repaint can never lose more than a second's words; and while a block has focus, the repaint keeps that block's live text and caret instead of replacing it. Enter in the title = done. A long-press on the picture offers *remove*. That keeps the in-place feel rather than adding an edit mode with a Done button, which I think is the wrong direction for a card that's meant to feel like your own page.

Did you hit something specific on your phone? If so tell me what you saw and I'll aim the fix at that first; otherwise I'll brief the four changes above as one subfeature of `cards` once `invite` lands.

Support and admin see a name box, a phone box and the word **invite** under their own card, drawn in Rust from a transient `invite` state key that the page half fills by fetching `GET users/invited`; a member's page shows nothing at all, and the decision is entirely server-side (`may:false`). `POST users/invite` appends `{name, phone, invited_by, invited}` to `users.json` under `with_store_lock`, refusing duplicates, empty names, malformed numbers and — a rig find — numbers typed without a country code, which normalise to a phone nobody could ever log in with. "Joined" is a stamp: `auth_verify` gained an outermost link that writes `joined: &lt;ms&gt;` on a successful verify, taken after the inner chain has released the lock. `POST users/uninvite` removes only an entry that carries `invited`, has never joined, and belongs to the caller (or the caller is admin). The guest list is written temp → 0600 → rename and is never written from a failed read; a broken `users.json` is answered 500 and logged by reason, with the store-health check deliberately ahead of the cookie check because with the list unreadable nobody is authed at all. All nine acceptance items pass, toggle proven both ways, and the surface passes 4a. No SMS is sent, as briefed.
> 
> Two things I decided rather than asked, both recorded in the spec: the button says **invite** (the copy rule says "invite / invited / joined and nothing else", so the story's reveal-then-send became one row and one tap), and uninvite refuses hand-written guest-list entries outright — stricter than the brief, so the app can never delete ash's own row.
>
